The Work and Torah Teaching of Rabbi David Oppenheim: His Life, His Famous Library and His Halakhic Method
In a historical setting marked by social, political and cultural upheavals in the Holy Roman Empire of the early modern period, the figure of Rabbi David Oppenheim (Maharar David Oppenheim; 5424 – 7 Tishrei 5497, 1664–1736) stands out as a canonical figure without precedent [cite: 1]. As one who served as head of the rabbinic court and as mara de-atra (local rabbinic authority) in the central communities of Nikolsburg and Prague, and as chief rabbi of the land of Bohemia on behalf of the imperial government, Rabbi David embodied the ideal of "Torah and greatness in one place" at its most splendid [cite: 1, 2, 3]. His life's work spanned forceful halakhic leadership, original rulings in the responsa "Nishal David", the building of a ramified network of ties with the elite of Court Jewry, and the creation of the largest and most important extant collection of Hebrew books and manuscripts of the early modern period [cite: 1, 4, 5]. This library, which served in his lifetime as a center of knowledge and a source of Torah and public authority, is housed today in the Bodleian Library at the University of Oxford and continues to serve as a central foundation for bibliographical and historical research [cite: 4, 6].
His Life, Lineage and Political and Social Standing
Rabbi David Oppenheim was born in the month of Sivan 5424 (June 1664) in the city of Worms (Vermayza) in Germany, one of the long-established centers of Ashkenazi Torah and culture [cite: 1, 7]. He was born to Rabbi Avraham Oppenheim, a member of a distinguished and very wealthy family whose family arteries were joined to the dynasties of wealth and influence of the "Court Jews" in the Holy Roman Empire [cite: 1, 2, 8]. His uncle was the famous magnate Rabbi Shmuel Oppenheimer, the financial manager and chief supplier of the imperial court in Vienna [cite: 1, 8]. Oppenheimer's ties with Prince Eugene of Savoy yielded, among other things, a spoil of rare Hebrew manuscripts that were brought from the Ottoman Empire after the Great Turkish War and passed on to Rabbi David [cite: 1, 8].
In his youth Rabbi David married Gnendel, the daughter of the Court Jew Lipman Katz (Leffmann Behrends) of Hanover [cite: 1, 5]. This marriage strengthened his economic position and gave him complete financial independence, which allowed him to devote his life to Torah study, to the leadership of communities and to the acquisition of books without depending on communal sources of livelihood [cite: 6, 7]. After the death of his wife Gnendel, he married a second time the daughter of Rabbi Binyamin Wolf Spira, head of the rabbinic court of Prague, a family bond that connected him deeply with the leadership of the community in Bohemia [cite: 2, 9].
Already in his youth Rabbi David stood out as an exceptional Torah prodigy. At about the age of 20 he was ordained to issue rulings, and at only 25 (in the month of Elul 5449, 1689) he was appointed rabbi of Nikolsburg and mara de-atra of the land of Moravia (Landesrabbiner) [cite: 1, 2, 5]. During the twenty years of his tenure in Nikolsburg he established his standing as one of the greatest halakhic authorities of his generation, as the sages of Europe sent him complex halakhic questions and sought his approbations for their books [cite: 1, 2]. In 5462 (1702) he moved to Prague, and in 5472 (1712) he was appointed chief rabbi of the city of Prague and the districts of Bohemia [cite: 2, 5, 10]. Prague was at that time one of the largest and most central Jewish communities in Europe, and his tenure there lasted about 24 years, until his death on 7 Tishrei 5497 (12 September 1736) at the age of 72 [cite: 1]. He was laid to rest in the Old Jewish Cemetery in Prague [cite: 1].
Rabbi David Oppenheim's standing went far beyond the bounds of classical rabbinic authority. Thanks to his extensive ties with the emperor's court in Vienna and to his family lineage, he served as an intercessor (shtadlan) and as a defender of the rights of the Jews in the realm, and the imperial government granted him an official letter of appointment as chief rabbi of the entire land of Bohemia, a position that gave him broad judicial and administrative powers [cite: 1, 2]. Alongside his work in Europe, Rabbi David stood at the head of the enterprises supporting the Jewish community in the Land of Israel, and he directed the mechanism for collecting funds and transferring economic support to the yeshivas and sages of Jerusalem, Safed and Hebron [cite: 3, 10]. In recognition of his decisive support and of his standing as the spiritual and material father of the Jews of the Land of Israel, the sages of Jerusalem bestowed on him the exalted title of honor "Nasi of the Land of Israel" (or "Nasi of Israel") [cite: 1, 3, 10]. Rabbi David printed copies of the letter of appointment he received from the emissaries of Jerusalem and distributed them, as part of establishing his authority over all of Jewry [cite: 11].

His Teachers, His Torah Connections and His Network of Influence
Rabbi David Oppenheim grew up in the splendid study halls of Ashkenaz and France in the 17th century, and his Torah education combined the long-established Ashkenazi traditions of learning with the new scholarly analysis that had developed in Central Europe. His principal teacher in his youth was Rabbi Gershon Ashkenazi (author of the responsa "Avodat ha-Gershuni"), who served as rabbi in the city of Metz [cite: 1, 2, 10]. From him Rabbi David received the method of thorough and practical halakhic analysis. In addition, he studied with Rabbi Yitzchak Binyamin Wolf of Landsberg (author of "Nachalat Binyamin"), who was one of the greatest teachers in Ashkenaz and deeply influenced his approach to analytical study and to teaching [cite: 1, 2]. Later he strengthened his studies with Rabbi Yaakov Sak Ashkenazi (father of Rabbi Tzvi Hirsch Ashkenazi, the "Chacham Tzvi"), a period of study that laid the foundation for his friendship with the great figures of the generation, and with Rabbi Binyamin Wolf Epstein in the city of Friedberg, with whom he completed his course of studies before he was appointed to the rabbinate [cite: 1].
Rabbi David's Torah and social network was among the most ramified and influential in Europe. Already in his youth he formed a deep friendship with Rabbi Yair Chaim Bacharach (author of the responsa "Chavot Yair"), and he maintained a rich Torah correspondence with him [cite: 1, 5]. His family ties wove him into the elite of the Torah world of his generation. Rabbi Yaakov Reischer (author of "Shevut Yaakov") was his brother-in-law, and in his books he addressed Rabbi David in expressions of exceeding praise and admiration, such as "my beloved master, my brother-in-law, the great Gaon famed in every corner and region... glory of the generation" and "master of the children of the Diaspora" [cite: 1, 10]. His renowned son-in-law, who married his daughter, was Rabbi Chaim Yonah Teomim (author of "Kuntres R. Chaim Yonah"), one of the greatest scholars and halakhic authorities in Prague [cite: 1, 2, 10]. He was likewise close by family to Rabbi Yonatan Eybeschutz during the latter's stay in Prague [cite: 9]. His only son, Rabbi Yosef Oppenheim, who served as head of the rabbinic court of Holleschau, married the daughter of the famous Court Jew Rabbi Shimshon Wertheimer of Vienna, thereby uniting the two most powerful families of leadership and wealth in European Jewry [cite: 1, 2]. This network served as a vital channel for the transmission of halakhic information, books and manuscripts, and for the coordination of communal and political policy throughout the empire [cite: 7, 11].
The Oppenheim Library – "Prince of the Press" and the Treasury of the Hebrew Book
The central achievement of Rabbi David Oppenheim, which fixed his place in the pages of the cultural history of the Jewish people, is the collection of books and manuscripts that he built [cite: 4, 5]. In a world in which books were an extremely precious and rare commodity, Rabbi David invested his vast fortune in creating the most comprehensive bibliographical collection of Hebrew literature of the early modern period [cite: 6, 12].
Already at the age of 22, in 1686, Rabbi David began to catalogue his private collection, which then numbered about 400 titles – an enormous achievement considering that in the entire world only about 2,000 Hebrew titles had been printed until then [cite: 7]. At the age of 24 the collection numbered 480 books [cite: 13], and at its peak it expanded to the huge dimensions of about 750 to 780 rare manuscripts and about 4,220 to 4,500 printed books [cite: 4, 14, 15]. This collection encompassed all fields of Jewish creativity: Bible, Talmud, halakha, Kabbalah, philosophy, festival prayer books (machzorim), homiletics, poetry and Old Yiddish literature [cite: 7, 14].
Rabbi David's methods of acquisition and collecting were planned and complex. He dispatched agents and emissaries throughout Europe, the Balkans and the Land of Israel to locate rare books [cite: 12]. At the same time, he kept a staff of private scribes and copyists, such as the scribe Azriel of Krotoszyn, who copied for him dozens of rare works and manuscripts that could not be purchased [cite: 11]. Moreover, Rabbi David financed many printers in Europe and supplied them with high-quality fine paper (and sometimes even parchment) so that they would print unique copies for him (Deluxe copies) [cite: 1]. Thanks to this, there survived in his library the only copies in the world of books and pamphlets all of whose other copies were lost [cite: 1, 14]. To mark his ownership, he developed an elaborate personal bookplate (Ex-Libris), and he made use of royal symbols and biblical figures, in particular King David, to express the conception of the "crown of Torah" combined with leadership [cite: 7].
Prague, which was under the rule of the House of Habsburg and the strong Catholic influence of the Jesuit order, suffered from severe censorship and from the uprooting of Hebrew books [cite: 13]. As rabbi of the community, Rabbi David understood that the judgments and bans of the imperial censorship might endanger his precious collection [cite: 13]. He therefore took an exceptional strategic step and stored his entire enormous library in the city of Hanover, in the house of his father-in-law Leffmann Katz, which was protected under the Protestant principality of Hanover [cite: 1, 16]. Throughout all his years as rabbi in Prague, his library stood hundreds of kilometers away from him. Rabbi David used to travel frequently to Hanover to consult his books, and he made use of emissaries and scribes who brought him specific manuscripts according to his needs of study and halakhic ruling [cite: 10, 11].
After his death in 1736, the library passed into the ownership of his son Rabbi Yosef, and afterwards into the hands of his granddaughter and her husband, who lived in Hildesheim [cite: 2, 11]. The family sank into debt and used the library as collateral for loans [cite: 11]. For decades the library stood up for sale, and sums far lower than its estimated value were offered for it (original estimate: 150,000 thalers) [cite: 5]. In 1829 the collection was purchased in its entirety by the Bodleian Library at the University of Oxford for a sum of 2,080 pounds sterling (about 9,000 thalers) [cite: 4, 5]. This purchase at a stroke doubled Oxford's collection of Hebrew manuscripts and made it one of the most important centers in the world for Jewish studies [cite: 4]. The scholars of the "Wissenschaft des Judentums" (Science of Judaism) in Europe, headed by Leopold Zunz, lamented the departure of the treasure beyond the bounds of the Jewish center in Europe, but thanks to this purchase the collection has been preserved in its entirety to our day [cite: 5]. The modern scholar Joshua Teplitsky devoted his comprehensive book Prince of the Press (2019) to the library and to the work of Rabbi David [cite: 7, 11, 17, 18].

The Torah Enterprise, His Works and His Halakhic Method
Alongside being a book collector and a public leader, Rabbi David Oppenheim was a halakhic authority of the first rank and a Torah innovator [cite: 1]. He composed about twenty books on halakha, aggadah and commentary, but in his humility – and out of a striving to reach perfection and maximal precision – he did not print most of his works in his lifetime, and they remained in manuscript [cite: 1, 2]. Rabbi David used to give his books titles containing his name ("David") [cite: 2].

The halakhic rulings of Rabbi David Oppenheim are characterized by a fusion of classical Ashkenazi scholarship with a public outlook and a deep sense of social responsibility. He did not regard halakha merely as abstract dialectics (pilpul), but as a practical instrument for leading the community and safeguarding the rights of the needy.
One of the famous rulings that illustrate his halakhic method concerns the law of divorcing a woman who has become insane (a shotah) [cite: 21]. The Gaon Rabbi Naftali Katz (head of the rabbinic court of Posen and Frankfurt) ruled that it is permitted to accept a bill of divorce (get) on behalf of a woman who is "completely insane" so that she will be considered unmarried, on the view that divorce is a "benefit" for her [cite: 21]. Rabbi David Oppenheim came out forcefully against this permission, and ruled in the responsa "Nishal David" (Even ha-Ezer, section 33) that such a get is void by Torah law [cite: 21]. In his legal analysis he established that an insane woman's get cannot be taken from her, since she is unable to guard her get or herself, and by Torah law she has no capacity of acquisition and no "hand", and therefore the get does not take effect [cite: 21]. Alongside the formal argument, Rabbi David raised a normative ethical-social reason: if an insane woman were divorced, those around her would treat her as unmarried, and this would lead to her being abandoned and treated "in a lawless manner" [cite: 21]. This analysis combines meticulous legal analysis with the protection of the weak in society. This ruling was later supported by his brother-in-law, Rabbi Yaakov Reischer, and by the author of the book "Panim Me'irot", and became a cornerstone of the laws of marriage [cite: 21].
Another example of his principled stance occurred in 1715, when the Habsburg authorities in Prague tried to compel Rabbi David Oppenheim to serve as the official censor of all Hebrew books printed in the city, in order to ensure that they contained no content against Christianity [cite: 13]. Rabbi David firmly and wisely refused to fill this role, and in his official reply to the authorities he argued that because of his advanced age, the weakness of his eyesight and the burden of his rabbinic duties, he was unable to examine the books [cite: 13]. Behind this diplomatic explanation stood a deep halakhic and public conception: Rabbi David refused to turn the seat of the rabbinate into an arm of government censorship, knowing that agreeing to this would place on him criminal and religious responsibility for every printed word and would harm the freedom of Jewish study and printing [cite: 13].
His Students, Torah Patronage and His Legacy for Generations
In Prague Rabbi David headed a large yeshiva that drew hundreds of young men and married scholars from all over Ashkenaz and Poland [cite: 2, 11]. He used his private library as an exceptional pedagogical aid: during his daily lessons, he used to bring before his students rare manuscripts and early printed editions of the Talmud and the halakhic authorities in order to establish precise readings and to examine the development of halakha [cite: 11]. Students and sages from all over Europe turned to him in letters to obtain permission to come and consult the manuscripts in his possession for the composition of their books [cite: 11].
Rabbi David's great wealth served as a central fund of support for the world of the Hebrew book, and many authors who suffered from abject poverty found with him a warm home and full funding for printing their books [cite: 2, 20]. A prominent example of this patronage is his support of the kabbalist Rabbi Moshe of Prague, author of the kabbalistic work "Va-Yakhel Moshe" [cite: 1]. Rabbi David hosted Rabbi Moshe in his home, supported him for years and enabled him to compose and print his book without worries about livelihood [cite: 1]. In addition, Rabbi David's approbations for books were regarded as a mark of quality of the first rank, and authors sent him their manuscripts in order to obtain his approbation, which ensured the book's circulation [cite: 2].
The legacy of Rabbi David Oppenheim extends along several central axes of influence. First, the gathering and management of his collection prevented the loss of hundreds of unique manuscripts and early printed books, which today form the core of the Hebrew collection in the Bodleian Library in Oxford [cite: 4, 14]. Second, his rulings in the responsa "Nishal David" and in his manuscripts continue to serve as a source of authority for halakhic decisors in recent generations, particularly in intricate questions of Even ha-Ezer and Choshen Mishpat [cite: 21]. Finally, his model of leadership represented the peak of Court Jewry: Rabbi David proved that wealth and influence in royal courts could directly serve the fortification of the world of Torah, the strengthening of the communities and the protection of the Jewish community in the Land of Israel [cite: 3, 8, 10, 12].
Summary and Conclusions
The figure of Rabbi David Oppenheim stands as one of the pillars of the culture of the book and of Jewish leadership in the transition from the early modern period to the modern period [cite: 7, 11]. The combination of his economic, family and political circumstances, together with his diligence in Torah and his halakhic genius, enabled him to create a life's work of historical dimensions [cite: 1, 3, 6].
His enormous library was not the pastime of a wealthy collector, but a strategic instrument for leadership, research and halakhic ruling [cite: 7, 12]. Through the mechanism of acquisition, copying and preservation that he created, Rabbi David established a center of knowledge that connected the sages of Ashkenaz, Sepharad and the Land of Israel [cite: 7, 12]. His judicious decision to store his collections in Hanover became a model of strategic planning in the face of religious and imperial censorship [cite: 13, 16]. Today, when the manuscripts and books of Rabbi David Oppenheim are studied in yeshivas and universities alike, his name is engraved not only as "master of the children of the Diaspora" and as "Nasi of the Land of Israel", but also as the "Prince of the Press" who rescued and preserved the memory of Hebrew writing for generations [cite: 1, 3, 7].
